chapter.title: Catching the agent when it is wrong

cards.body: On day 3, your agent tells you a rival just deleted every price on their site. They didn't: the page failed to load, and your clipper reported a blank sheet as news. A good clipping service fixes this with **three quick checks before the note reaches your desk**, not with more trust in the clipper.
cards.simpler: On day 3, your agent tells you a rival just wiped every price off their site. That isn't true. The page just failed to load, and your agent reported the blank page as news. Think of the agent as a helper who clips news for you. The fix isn't trusting the helper more. It's **three quick checks before the note reaches your desk**.

cards.prompt: Your clipper's note says: "Rival Nimbus cut every plan from their pricing page." The clipping stapled to it is one line long: "Please verify you are human." What most likely happened?

options.text: Nimbus really removed all its plans overnight
The page didn't load properly, so the agent compared a real page with a blank one
Nimbus moved its prices to a different page

whyNot.a: That's the note's claim, not the evidence: the clipping shows a blocked page, not a pricing page.
whyNot.c: That's a possible real change, not what this clipping shows: a one-line "verify you are human" page means the download was blocked.

cards.reteach: The agent can only compare what it downloaded. If the download is a block page, every real line looks "removed", and the summary dutifully reports a disaster. Look at the clipping before you believe the note.

cards.title: Checks 1 and 2: the paper and the news
cards.body:
**Check 1: did the fetch work?** A *fetch* is the agent downloading the page. Sometimes it gets a cookie banner, an error, or a "verify you are human" wall instead. The quick test: is today's copy roughly the size of yesterday's, and does it contain a word you expect, like "$" or "per month"? If not, the agent writes "fetch failed" and stops.

Check 2: is the diff empty? If nothing changed, the note says "no changes" and skips the model entirely. Ask a model what changed in nothing, and it will sometimes find something anyway, like a clipper who hates going home empty-handed.
cards.simpler: Check 1: **did the page download properly?** Sometimes your agent gets a cookie pop-up, an error, or a "prove you are human" screen instead. Quick test: is today's copy about as big as yesterday's, and does it include a word you expect, like "$" or "per month"? If not, the agent writes "fetch failed" and stops. Check 2: if nothing changed, the note says "no changes" and skips the model. Asked about nothing, a model sometimes invents something anyway.

cards.title: The 312-character price cut
cards.body: Tuesday, 7:02am. Maya's summary says Acme "removed its Pro plan and all pricing." She opens the saved copy: 312 characters, mostly the words "Please verify you are human." Yesterday's copy was 9,400 characters. The model did its job perfectly; it was just handed a torn newspaper. **A rule like "under half of yesterday's size means stop"** would have caught it before breakfast.
cards.simpler: Tuesday, 7:02am. Maya's summary says Acme "removed its Pro plan and all pricing." Maya opens the saved copy of the page. It's 312 characters long, mostly the words "Please verify you are human." Yesterday's copy was 9,400 characters. The model did nothing wrong. It was just handed a torn newspaper. **A rule like "under half of yesterday's size means stop"** would have caught this before breakfast.

cards.prompt: Your agent fetches 4 pages. Three look normal. The fourth, Corva's changelog, is 280 characters today and was 6,100 yesterday. What should the agent do with Corva?

options.text: Summarise the diff as usual and let you decide
Mark it "fetch failed", skip the summary for that page, and try again tomorrow
Compare today's copy with last week's instead of yesterday's

whyNot.a: That's trusting the note over the clipping: a 280-character copy will make almost every line look removed.
whyNot.c: That's changing the comparison, not the copy: today's download is still broken, whichever day you compare it to.

cards.reteach: A copy that shrank by more than 95% overnight is almost always a failed download, not news. The agent should catch it at the door, say so plainly, and keep it away from the model. One honest "fetch failed" beats one confident wrong summary.

cards.title: Check 3: every claim has a clipping
cards.body:
In chapter 5 you told the model to quote the source line for each claim. Now the agent checks that quote: it searches today's saved copy for the exact words, the way you'd press Ctrl+F on a page. Found means verified. Not found means the claim gets a flag: *unverified*.

You'd think a better-written summary needs less checking. It's the opposite. **A smooth sentence with no matching line is the most dangerous thing in your inbox**, because it reads exactly like a true one.

So the note on your desk shows each claim beside its clipping. Checking one takes seconds.
cards.simpler: In chapter 5, you told the model to quote the source line for each claim. Now the agent checks it by searching today's saved page for those exact words, like pressing Ctrl+F. Found means verified. Not found means the claim is marked "unverified." **A smooth sentence with no matching line is the most dangerous thing in your inbox**, because it reads just like a true one. So each claim sits beside its quote. Checking takes seconds.

cards.body: Sam's agent flagged "fetch failed" on the same rival 5 mornings in a row; their site blocks robots. Annoyed, he deleted the fetch check. On day 9 his summary announced that rival had shut down its whole product, and he forwarded it to his co-founder before lunch. The tell: **if you've ignored the same warning 3 days running, fix the source** (swap the page or drop it), not the alarm.
cards.simpler: Sam's agent flagged "fetch failed" on the same rival five mornings in a row, because that site blocks robots. Annoyed, Sam deleted the check. On day 9, the summary said the rival had shut down its whole product, and Sam forwarded it to a co-founder before lunch. The lesson: **if you've ignored the same warning 3 days running, fix the source**. Swap the page or drop it. Don't silence the alarm.

cards.prompt: Today's note says: "Beta Co added a Teams plan at $49 per user a month," quoting "Teams: $49 / user / month". What tells you this claim is real?

options.text: The sentence is specific and includes an exact price
The quoted line appears word for word in today's saved copy of Beta Co's pricing page
The diff for Beta Co wasn't empty today

whyNot.a: That's sounding sure, not being right: an invented claim can be just as specific.
whyNot.c: That's check 2, not check 3: a non-empty diff says something changed, not that this claim is what changed.

cards.reteach: Each claim needs its own clipping. The only proof is the quoted words, found in the real saved page. Specific, confident and "something changed" can all be true of a wrong summary too.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Your agent can be wrong in 3 ways: it read a broken page, it was asked about nothing, or it described a line that isn't there. So it **checks the page size, skips empty diffs, and searches the saved copy for every quote** before the note reaches you.

Next: why one weekly note can tell you more than seven daily ones.
cards.simpler: Your agent can be wrong in 3 ways. It read a broken page. It was asked about nothing. Or it described a line that isn't there. So before a note reaches you, it **checks the page size, skips empty changes, and searches the saved copy for every quote**. Next: why one weekly note can tell you more than seven daily ones.

cards.body: Open one summary your agent wrote this week. Pick a single claim, then open that page's saved copy and press Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac) to search for its quoted line. Did you find it?
cards.simpler: Open one summary your agent wrote this week. Pick one claim from it. Then open the saved copy of that page and press Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac) to **search for the quoted line**. It's like checking a news story against the original paper. Did you find it?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now read one day's summary, trace each claim back to its source line, and spot a failed fetch or an invented claim in under 2 minutes.
